chapter: Army band, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday and the 1950s
title: Leading the 732nd Military Police Band at Camp Desplaines, 1942-43
summary: Louis Armstrong turned down bandmaster of the Joliet camp band under Wayne King and recommended Horace. He led a 42-piece band including Fats Waller's saxophonist Jackie Fields, and got letters from draft-eligible musicians.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I don't know why I lost that. Well, maybe we can get back to that. The other day, we talked a little bit -- I'm leaping ahead now to the early Forties. We had talked about the fact that John Hammond had helped you get

this recording session together using some of the musicians from Nat Towles' band, and that apparently took place in late '40 and -- 1941 and so on. Then in 1942, you did go into the army, and we talked about that the other day, and according to my information here from November '42 to August of '43, you were in the army and you were the leader of the 732nd Military Police Band.
And you said that was in Illinois -- where?
Camp Desplaines. And that was under Wayne King's supervision. He was the one that --
Was he stationed there at the camp?
He was in Chicago. He was connected with the armed forces at that time.
So he probably had a number of different bands in different posts that were --
(Unaudible) It was first offered to Louis Armstrong, and he turned it down -- as the bandmaster, you know.
And he recommended me to Wayne King.
So Wayne King came out to see me and said, 'We're gonna have a

camp in Joliet, Illinois, and they needed a leader that would be made bandmaster, you know, so this is exactly what happened. So I played all the service clubs and what not, and we had this great 42 piece band.
Were there any name musicians in that band?

Really, not outstanding, no. But I did have musicians from some great bands, like Fats Waller's band. I had his first saxophone player, Jackie Fields out of New York City that he was drafted as 1A. I don't know if we mentioned this a few days ago, but during that time there was such a thing in the army requesting a guy, if he was 1A and a musician, and you were given a letter of authority where this guy was coming from the service center right directly to you, and man, I began to get letters from all over the country from guys who were 1A. "I'm a saxophonist." "Please call me."
Yeah. "Please call me. I want to get in your band. I know I'm gonna be drafted. I'm 1A, and I'd like to do this, you know, so we found quite a great group there in Joliet.
